name: Breathwork

image.caption: Rosanna Holmström, certified breathwork facilitator and athletic breath coach

lead: Breathwork is an umbrella term for practices that use deliberate breathing patterns to change how a person feels. It covers slow, paced techniques such as box breathing and cyclic sighing, and more intense styles such as holotropic breathwork, rebirthing and the Wim Hof method, which involve rapid breathing and breath holds.

People in self-improvement and appearance communities use it as a stress and recovery tool. The chain they describe runs from lower stress and better sleep to calmer skin, less tension in the face and jaw, steadier energy for training and a more composed presence. A 2023 meta-analysis of randomised trials found breathwork associated with lower self-reported stress, with a small-to-medium effect.

paras: Sessions range from a few minutes of slow breathing at a desk or before bed to hour-long guided group sessions, sometimes with music and a sitter. Faster styles are usually taught by a trained facilitator, and some people combine breathing with cold exposure. Effects on mood and arousal are reported within a single session.

Slow breathing is generally described as low-risk. Fast, hyperventilation-style breathwork can cause tingling, cramping in the hands or face, dizziness and, in some cases, brief loss of consciousness. Clinicians list heart disease, high blood pressure, seizure disorders, severe asthma, glaucoma and some mental health conditions as reasons to avoid intense styles, and the Wim Hof method specifically warns against practising in water.

angle.text: Breathwork changes physiological arousal during and after a session. People use it to ease stress, which they associate with better sleep, less visible tension and more energy for training; it does not directly alter facial or body structure.

lead: Breathwork is a general name for practices that use conscious control of breathing to influence mental, emotional or physical state [1]. The term is used for slow paced breathing, for yoga-derived pranayama, and for more intense New Age systems such as Stanislav Grof's holotropic breathwork and Leonard Orr's rebirthing, which began in the 1970s [1].

Within appearance and lifestyle communities, breathwork is used mostly as an indirect aid: practitioners describe it as a way to manage stress, sleep better and recover from training, which they connect with clearer skin, less facial tension, better posture and a more relaxed look. Related entries in this wiki cover the nasal-breathing and mouth-posture theories that discuss breathing and facial structure; those are separate from breathwork as a stress practice.

Research is growing. A 2023 meta-analysis of twelve randomised controlled trials with 785 adults found breathwork associated with lower self-reported stress compared with control conditions (g = -0.35) [2]. Reviews describe fragmented research across many techniques [3][4]. A randomised trial found that five-minute daily breathing exercises improved mood and reduced arousal, with cyclic sighing performing best [5].

Free to self-practice; group sessions vary

paras: Practices differ widely. Slow, paced approaches such as box breathing (equal-length inhale, hold, exhale) and cyclic sighing (emphasising a long exhale) are short and can be done sitting at a desk [5]. High-ventilation practices involve sustained fast breathing and are the basis of holotropic breathwork and many group sessions [3][1]. Participants in guided sessions typically lie down and breathe for around an hour, often with music and a sitter who provides support [1].
The Wim Hof Method, developed by Dutch athlete Wim Hof, combines breathing exercises with cold exposure and meditation [6].

Rebirthing was devised by Leonard Orr in the 1970s, who described reliving his own birth in a bath and then developed a method aimed at releasing repressed childhood memories. Stanislav Grof developed holotropic breathwork as a successor to LSD-assisted therapy after legal psychedelic research was restricted in the late 1960s [1]. Breathing control also has older roots in yogic pranayama and in Chinese xingqi practices [1].
Interest in breathwork rose sharply in the 2010s and 2020s through wellness media, apps and influencers, including the Wim Hof Method and writers who popularised nasal breathing.

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and appearance culture
paras: Practitioners present breathwork as part of a recovery stack alongside sleep, cold exposure and training. Those who use it say lower stress shows up as less jaw clenching, steadier sleep and better skin, and some use it before photos or social events to feel composed. These are users' reports; published trials measure stress, mood and arousal rather than appearance.

A 2023 meta-analysis in Scientific Reports of twelve randomised trials found a significant small-to-medium reduction in self-reported stress with breathwork versus controls, with most studies at moderate risk of bias [2]. A randomised trial in Cell Reports Medicine compared three daily five-minute breathing exercises (cyclic sighing, box breathing and a hyperventilation-style exercise) with mindfulness meditation over a month; the breathing conditions improved mood and reduced physiological arousal [5]. Overviews of high-ventilation practices and technique comparisons describe shared nervous-system mechanisms and note that the field is fragmented [3][4].

Further trials have examined breathwork combined with cold immersion [7] and online conscious connected breathwork for anxiety [8]. A 2024 meta-analysis of Wim Hof studies, summarised by Wikipedia, found possible reductions in inflammation but rated the evidence as very low quality, with small samples and high risk of bias [6].

Common effects of fast breathing include sleepiness, tingling in the hands, feet or face, cramping around the mouth and a distressing altered state for some people. Breathwork is generally considered safe with a skilled practitioner but is contraindicated for people with cardiovascular disease, glaucoma, high blood pressure, mental illness, severe asthma or seizure disorders [1]. After a 1993 report raised concerns about hyperventilation triggering seizures or psychosis in vulnerable people, the Findhorn Foundation suspended its breathwork programme [1].

The Wim Hof method's breathing can cause hyperventilation leading to brief unconsciousness; in water this can be fatal. Deaths have been reported among practitioners, including drownings in 2015 and 2016, and Hof's official materials advise practising in safe locations [6].

Edzard Ernst describes breathwork, including rebirthing, as alternative medicine, and critics have called some forms non-scientific; a 2006 expert panel rated rebirthing therapy as discredited [1]. Researchers more favourable to the field argue that slower breathing techniques share neurophysiological mechanisms that benefit wellbeing [4]. A 2018 review noted limited research linking physiological measures to psychological outcomes in healthy people [1].

lore.intro: Breathwork appears in appearance and self-improvement communities as a stress, sleep and recovery tool, often alongside cold exposure and nasal-breathing practice.
